story: In 1971, Joan Miró authored his own poetry and created a series of original color lithographs to accompany the text for the publication *Le Lézard aux plumes d'or*. Publisher Louis Broder brought the project to completion in Paris, issuing the portfolio as an illustrated edition alongside printer Mourlot.

Joan Miró authored his own poetic text and paired it with a suite of color lithographs for the illustrated book project Le Lézard aux plumes d'or. Publisher Louis Broder released the completed work in Paris in 1971. Miró worked directly with the print shop Mourlot to produce the edition, transferring his calligraphy and imagery directly onto the stones rather than using lithography merely as a tool for reproduction.

In 1967, Joan Miró and the master printmakers at Atelier Mourlot completed a full suite of color lithographs for *Le Lézard aux plumes d'or*. Shortly after printing finished, Miró and his publisher discovered a manufacturing flaw in the paper that altered and distorted the colors of the prints. While reference catalogues originally recorded that this defective 1967 edition was completely destroyed, surviving impressions eventually resurfaced decades later. Miró moved forward with the project despite the setback, ultimately issuing the completed illustrated book in 1971.

Joan Miró authored the text and created the lithographs for Le Lézard aux plumes d'or in 1971, which was published by Louis Broder and printed by Mourlot Frères in Paris. Boston-based art collector Boris Fridman acquired twentieth-century illustrated artists' books and presented his holdings, including this work, to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. The museum included the volume in its exhibition Picasso, Miró, Dalí: Unbound to feature works drawn from Fridman's collection.
